summary: Extends Proxy Mobile IPv6 with IPv4 support. It lets a mobile node keep an IPv4 home address while moving, and allows the network elements to exchange signaling over an IPv4 transport. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: You keep your old-style phone number when you move around town, and the helpers can talk over old-style lines too.

subtitle: Lets a Proxy Mobile IPv6 network give phones an IPv4 address that follows them, and run its own signaling over IPv4 links.

tldr.problem: Proxy Mobile IPv6 (RFC 5213) only offers IPv6 home addresses and requires an IPv6 network between its mobility entities, but real networks mix IPv4 and IPv6.
tldr.mechanism: New Proxy Mobile IPv6 options let the mobile access gateway ask the local mobility anchor for an IPv4 home address, with DHCP handing it to the node. Separately, signaling and tunnels can run over IPv4, with UDP encapsulation and optional IPsec ESP.
tldr.outcome: A node can keep the same IPv4 address while moving anywhere in the domain, and the two features can be deployed independently. RFC 5844 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no replacement.

today: RFC 5844 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 5213 and reuses ideas from RFC 5555.

sections.title: Why Proxy Mobile IPv6 Needs IPv4
sections.content:
The move from IPv4 to IPv6 is a long process, so a mobile node in a Proxy Mobile IPv6 domain may be IPv4-only, IPv6-only or dual-stack, and the network between the mobile access gateway (MAG) and the local mobility anchor (LMA) may be IPv4 or IPv6. The base protocol, RFC 5213, gives IPv6 home address mobility and requires an IPv6 transport network between the mobility entities.

RFC 5844 adds two independent features. IPv4 home address mobility lets a node obtain an IPv4 address and keep using it from any access network in the domain, without needing an IPv6 address. IPv4 transport support lets the MAG and LMA exchange signaling over an IPv4 network. A deployment may enable either or both.

The document assumes the MAG and LMA are dual-stack, that the signaling is always Proxy Mobile IPv6, and that the MAG is the node's IPv4 default router. A MAG using a private IPv4 address behind NAT toward the LMA is not supported.
sections.eli5: The old network did one kind of addressing. This document teaches it to also handle the older kind, so people keep the same address as they roam.

sections.title: Terms and Building Blocks
sections.content:
The RFC defines a few new terms on top of those in RFC 3775 and RFC 5213.

  • IPv4-MN-HoA: the IPv4 home address of the mobile node, anchored at its LMA.
  • IPv4-Proxy-CoA: the IPv4 address on the MAG's egress interface. With IPv4 transport it is the registered care-of address and the tunnel endpoint.
  • IPv4-LMAA: the IPv4 address on the LMA's egress interface, where the MAG sends Proxy Binding Updates.
  • Selective de-registration: removing only the IPv4 home address, or only the IPv6 prefixes, of a session.

All addresses of one interface, IPv4 and IPv6, are managed in one mobility session with a single Binding Cache entry. A node with several interfaces gets a unique IPv4 address for each. The document borrows from Dual-Stack Mobile IPv6 (RFC 5555), including the F flag and the NAT Detection option, but IPsec works differently because security associations belong to the MAG rather than to each node.
sections.eli5: There are a few new name tags: one for the traveler's address, one for the helper at the door, and one for the home base that keeps track of everyone.

sections.title: IPv4 Home Address Mobility
sections.content:
When a node attaches, the MAG consults its policy profile and, if IPv4 is needed, sends a Proxy Binding Update (PBU) with exactly one IPv4 Home Address Request option. Setting the address to all zeros asks the LMA to allocate one. A non-zero address asks for that specific one. Home Network Prefix options appear only if IPv6 mobility is also wanted, and at least one of the two option kinds must be present.

The LMA checks the request. It rejects with a Proxy Binding Acknowledgement (PBA) if the node is not authorized for IPv4 service or for the requested address, if there is more than one request option, or if it lacks resources. On success it creates one Binding Cache entry for both IPv4 and IPv6, sets up a bidirectional tunnel and an IPv4 host route, and replies with status 0, an IPv4 Home Address Reply option and an IPv4 Default-Router Address option.

The LMA advertises a connected route for the node's IPv4 home address or subnet, and forwards packets for it through the tunnel. After a handoff, the new MAG repeats the registration and the old forwarding state is removed. The MAG SHOULD answer the node's ARP requests, using Proxy ARP for destinations on the home subnet.
sections.eli5: The helper at the door asks the home base for an address for the visitor. The home base picks one, remembers it, and sends the visitor's mail through a private tunnel to wherever they are.

sections.title: New Options and Status Codes
sections.content:
Four new mobility options carry the IPv4 information. Each of the first three has a Length of 6 and an alignment requirement of 4n; the DHCP Support Mode option has a Length of 2.

  • IPv4 Home Address Request (type 36): sent by the MAG in the PBU, with a 6-bit prefix length and the requested address, 0.0.0.0 meaning allocate one.
  • IPv4 Home Address Reply (type 37): sent in the PBA, with a Status field, a prefix length and the assigned address. Values 0 to 127 mean success and 128 to 255 mean failure.
  • IPv4 Default-Router Address (type 38): the node's default router address.
  • IPv4 DHCP Support Mode (type 39): a 1-bit S flag, where 0 means the MAG acts as a DHCP relay and 1 means a DHCP server.

Four new PBA status codes are defined, all above 128, and IANA assigned the two UDP ports used later.
sections.eli5: The messages get four new little forms to fill in: one to ask for an address, one to answer, one to name the exit door, and one to say who hands out the address.

sections.title: Handing Out the Address with DHCP
sections.content:
The node can learn its IPv4 address through any standard mechanism, but the RFC spells out DHCP, with two supported layouts. In both, the mobile node's DHCP lease must survive handoffs, so the MAG presents a stable identity. Nodes SHOULD generate their Client-identifier per RFC 4361.

DHCP server on the MAG. After the PBU and PBA succeed and the tunnel is up, the MAG sends a DHCPOFFER with the home address, plus the Subnet Mask and Router options. The Server Identifier is set to the node's default router address, or a fixed address common across the domain, so renewals after a handoff reach the new MAG, which answers with DHCPACK or DHCPNACK.

DHCP relay on the MAG. A DHCP server sits elsewhere in the domain. The relay adds the Relay Agent Information option with the assigned address as a hint in the Agent Remote ID sub-option, and drops any DHCPOFFER whose address differs from what the LMA assigned. DHCP messages crossing administrative boundaries need to be secured.
sections.eli5: Once the home base has picked the address, the helper at the door tells the visitor about it using the usual address-giving ritual, so the visitor does not need to know anything special.

sections.title: IPv4 Transport for Signaling and Tunnels
sections.content:
RFC 5213 could already run over IPv4 by using an IPv6-over-IPv4 tunnel, but that adds 40 octets of overhead to each of the node's tunneled packets. The extensions here avoid that by sending signaling directly over IPv4. The MAG and LMA must be reachable by IPv4 addresses of the same scope. Private addresses are fine as long as there is no NAT between them.

The PBU and PBA lose their IPv6 header and the Mobility Header travels in UDP, with the Mobility Header checksum set to zero and the UDP checksum used. The PBU goes to destination port 5436, and the PBA uses source port 5436. Data tunnels can use plain IPv4, IPv4-UDP (port 5437), IPv4-UDP-TLV or IPv4-GRE. The LMA picks IPv4-UDP when the F flag is set in the PBU, and otherwise plain IPv4. If the F flag is set but the LMA flag AcceptForcedIPv4UDPEncapsulationRequest is 0, the request is rejected with status 129.

The MAG flag ForceIPv4UDPEncapsulationSupport controls whether the MAG sets the F flag. Both flags default to 0.
sections.eli5: If the roads between the helpers are old-style roads, they can still pass their notes along those roads directly, instead of wrapping every parcel in extra packaging.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
All the security considerations of Proxy Mobile IPv6, Mobile IPv6 and Dual-Stack Mobile IPv6 apply. The new options travel in PBU and PBA messages, and the protection that the base protocol already requires for those messages is sufficient for them.

With IPv4 transport, signaling can be protected with IPsec ESP. The RFC gives example Security Policy Database entries: transport-mode ESP for UDP port 5436 traffic between the IPv4-Proxy-CoA and the IPv4-LMAA, and tunnel-mode ESP for payload packets in the tunnel. IPsec processing happens before the message reaches Proxy Mobile IPv6.
sections.eli5: The new notes need the same locked envelopes as the old ones, and the older-road notes can use locked envelopes too.
